reviews.text: "Peak for losers with no friends" Barda ended up being very well welcomed surprise. The inventory management and survival mechanics are surprisingly deep, forcing you to carefully balance supplies, hunger, fatigue, and risk during the climb. What makes it work so well is how polished and focused the overall design feels. It combines survival systems with almost board game-like decision making, which makes every choice feel important. A genuinely tense and rewarding experience that constantly kept me engaged. My only "complaint" is that I "beat" the game after the first run and felt like there should have been more and not just a weekly rerun. Maybe an ascension mode would work? I got this game as a freebie from a wonderful company, and I've enjoyed the time I've had playing this game. I treat it like a game of Solitare, good for when I'm bored and there's nothing else going on. I attempted to stream this on TikTok, and people enjoyed it, but it lacked enthusiasm. I will likely play this game again on rare occasions and enjoy it thoroughly, however it will never be a mainstay in my gaming rotation. Much kudos to the creator, I enjoy the artwork and the concept is quite cute. I hope they add more content to the game and release new games in the future. My biggest complaint would be the online presence of the creator, of whom attempted to garner attention for their game on TikTok, but completely ignores their messages. Thanks for this opportunity.

The objective is to carry your granddad’s ashes to the top of the mountain. Each run is random and built from nodes and regions where you can sometimes choose where to go next. Nodes are marked with icons so you can see what kind of event or challenge awaits you there, including climbing, fighting, looting, and light challenges. Each node you visit is a single screen with a few points you can interact with, and it can contain different types of challenges at the same time. The main challenge is always clearly shown with its icon, and you only need to complete that one to progress, while the rest are optional. Depending on the region, simply choosing to travel to the next node can come with a drawback. You might gain fatigue, which makes you get hungry faster, or fear, which can make items unusable. Hunger increases with every new node you enter, and if you do not manage it with food, it will eventually start to damage your health. A node also contains extra loot spots marked with a small diamond, which can sometimes be easy to miss on bright backgrounds. Clicking a loot spot with the left mouse button drops a few random items that you can place in your backpack, and it is always worth checking them whenever you see them. Items are your main tools for reaching the summit. You can technically progress through challenges without them, but you will face far more penalties and risks. The only exception are optional challenges that require specific items. If you do not have what you need, you will have to skip them. For all other challenges, you can either use an item by dragging it onto the challenge or attempt it on your own by right clicking it. Items come in several types, including food. You can quickly see if something in your inventory is useful by hovering over a challenge and checking for a highlight on matching items. In general, you will find ropes and pickaxes for climbing, swords and sharp objects for fighting, and candles and lanterns for light-based challenges. Some items can be used for more than one type of challenge. Each challenge has a number above it that represents its health, or the amount you need to fully clear it. Items also have their own strength value, and your goal is to reduce the challenge health to zero in a single attempt. This does not depend only on the item, since most of them have relatively low values. Your character also adds a strength bonus, which is a random value from one to four. If you manage to clear all the health in one attempt, you receive a reward such as loot, a new challenge, or safe travel without penalties. If you are unlucky and do not fully clear the challenge in one try, which will always happen if you rely only on your character without using items, you will receive a punishment tied to that node. The most common is scratch, which reduces item durability. You can also encounter madness, which changes item effects, or illness, which lowers item strength. Any item left outside your bag will be destroyed when you travel. Beyond backpack space limitations, items also have durability that decreases with each use. Food and certain consumables are an exception since they are used up immediately. Depending on the item, it may break completely and disappear, or it may remain broken in your inventory, allowing you to repair it later if you find the right tool. You can also reach repair nodes, which are special locations. Other special nodes include markets, where you can sell items you do not need and buy new ones, rest areas, where you can use items to remove negative effects or cook them to reduce hunger, and merchants, which let you choose one perk out of three. The first perk increases your backpack size. The second gives you a strap that lets you carry one item outside your bag, ideally a large one that takes up too much space. The third offers useful badges that grant special effects, such as protection from weather conditions or a chance to reduce hunger during travel. A merchant always appears after clearing a region or defeating a boss. A small layer of meta-progress comes from random quests you receive at the start of each run. If you complete them, you gain talent points. Once you collect enough, you can unlock new items and characters that appear during runs, expand the pool of available quests, and even start each run with two random items.

I'm not very good at roguelike games but I wanted to try Barda out because I'd never seen a roguelike inventory management game before. The gameplay is simple enough that you just keep things in your backpack that you will need to climb to the top BUT you're also having to deal with hunger and illness among other things. I died so many times to hunger that I was starting to get annoyed haha The explorer upgrades are simple and don't try to be too much. You do need to finish the quests to get more explorer points so that's a thing. Overall I can see this being a fun repeat game. Easily 100% completable. And if you want to be challenged without overly exerting yourself, this is a nice paced game for it.
It's small and it's lovely. A cozy sort of texture throughout a roguelite journey. Decisions, yes, but never too tough. I've enjoyed returning to it just to let its pleasant feelings wash over me.
Interesting take on a roguelite. Pretty chill not too challenging.

I won't refund because i believe that small indie gems like this deserve the players' support (besides, the game costs only 9$ ...). That being said, content is just way too slim and that's doing a disservice to the game. There's a lot of upgrades and items that most players will never interact with, just because the game is over so quickly. I finished the story first try on the demo build, then purchased the full game to see what else is available, and after losing a run, finished the story again. So in the span of only 2 hours (1 on the demo, 1 on the full build), i did 3 runs, 2 of which went all the way to the end. Sure, there's the infinite weekly challenge, but honestly, i believe the game would greatly benefit from a content update that would add new biomes, maybe some with higher difficulty. I would gladly spend more time on things that requires more tries, and make metaprogression actually useful (again, at the moment, you can easily finish the game without purchasing any of the upgrades, so it doesn't really feel like a "roguelite" in that sense). The music is great, the art is great, the core gameplay is nice, the item variety is good, the metaprogression system is robust, ... everything is there for the player to sink dozens of hours into the game, except for content. So TLDR : Great little gem, would definitely recommend it just because you can tell a lot of effort went into it, but held back by its lack of content.

Its great!.... as a proof of concept. Still chosing to upvote it if for no other reason than the gorgeous art. Gameplay wise, the idea is fun and its cool to have more roguelikes that aren't based on violence. However, the balance feels wildly off. My first win was just having the good drops at the right time while the losses often happen very early because you may get low drop areas with challenges that your items are not related to. I hope the devs are going to look into making this more about strategy than luck.

The dev probably underestimated how good we are at playing games, a lot of people were able to complete the goal of the game on their first try lol. The game seems to have some window scaling problem and full screen doesn't work by me when on linux so don't play on linux if you can avoid it. The opposite happens when I play on windows, I can't leave full screen there. Some small QoLs will definitely be appreciated but the game is quite nice can recommend.

I like the idea a lot. It's unique, it's daring and it's fresh! The exact things I am looking for, when purchasing games! Unfortunately, it is also janky, and I can not see it changing any time soon, since I feel the biggest issue is deeply rooted in the game's core. , although I would love to be proven wrong. The biggest issue is the hunger at the end of each stage resulting in messy situations, or placing an item at an exact position that blows the bag up and spits all the items out. Literal mess. I get that the game is all about organizing the bag, but at a certain point, it becomes very very sloppy and wasteful. In any case, huge props to the developer of the game for seeing the game through and pushing on for the 1.0 release!
The content is enough for just a couple of hours, but replaybility adds to it potentially 5-15 hours. I would play this more just because it is charming: visual style, effects, outstanding sountrack.
